title: The Great Agatha Christie - Should Be Canonical?
author: John Mark Reynolds
summary: Classical educator John Mark Reynolds makes the case that Agatha Christie -- arguably the best-selling novelist of all time -- has been systematically excluded from literary canons and 'great women writers' lists not for lack of merit but because her happiness, readability, conventional politics, and stylistic conservatism (including her comfortable use of 'he' as a default pronoun) make her uncongenial to the tastes that currently curate such lists. He argues her exclusion is doubly perverse because Christie's fiction is saturated with an essentially Christian moral worldview -- Poirot and Marple are unintelligible without Christian conceptions of morality and civilization -- yet she is too commercially successful and insufficiently obscure to interest secular literary advocates, and too divorced and doctrinally loose to satisfy religious fundamentalists, leaving her championed by almost no institutional camp. Reynolds contends her prose is genuinely difficult by contemporary standards (challenging vocabulary and sentence complexity relative to most graduate English majors today) while remaining fully accessible to a reader at an early-20th-century eighth-grade reading level, a combination he treats as evidence of real craft rather than mere commercial formula, and adds that her characters (Poirot, Marple) stand as equals to Arthur Conan Doyle's. The essay closes by quoting at length Christie's own reflection on the three-part structure of time -- the fleeting present, the improbable-plan-filled future, and memory as 'the bedrock of one's present life' -- offered as direct evidence of the literary sensibility Reynolds argues deserves canonical, not merely popular, status.
points: Reynolds's central claim is structural, not merely appreciative: Christie is excluded from both secular 'great women writers' lists (too commercially successful, too conventional) and from fundamentalist religious canons (divorced, doctrinally loose), leaving her championed by essentially no institutional gatekeeper despite arguably being the best-selling novelist of all time.

The essay treats Christie's fiction as inseparable from a specifically Christian moral framework, arguing Poirot and Marple are unintelligible as characters without an underlying Christian conception of morality and civilization -- reframing 'merely entertaining' detective fiction as load-bearing moral literature.

The claim that Christie's prose is genuinely more linguistically demanding (vocabulary, sentence complexity) than most contemporary graduate English majors encounter, while remaining fully accessible at an early-20th-century eighth-grade reading level, is used as evidence against the assumption that her broad popular readability implies a lack of literary craft.

The essay's closing move -- quoting Christie's own extended reflection on the three-part structure of time (present, future, and memory as 'the bedrock of one's present life') -- functions as the piece's own evidentiary exhibit for canonical-quality prose, letting Christie's own writing make the argument the essay has been building.
quotes: When you are given a list of women writers, excellent writers, you are not generally given the best selling writer who is a woman, because Agatha Christie, mayhap the best selling author of all time, somehow (usually) does not count as a woman.
She endures: nobody makes the era between World War I and World War II more comprehensible than Agatha Christie, even if she does not say what we wish she would say about it.

Agatha Christie is not Christian enough for the fundamentalists, but then the fundamentalists do not control much of anything in the English speaking world. Agatha Christie is deeply Christian (understand Marple and Poirot without Christian morality and civilization!) and moralistic, so those who normally promote the most obscure writers for the secular cause ignore her writing.

Mostly of course Christie could write and is still readable. She has a vocabulary and complexity of sentence structure challenging to most graduate English majors today, but if you can read English at a (1930's) eighth grade level, she sings.
Christie was womanly, brilliant, conservative, and cosmopolitan. If you think this cannot be done, read And Then There Was None.

We should love and learn from any author who can say this about time: "Life seems to me to consist of three parts: the absorbing and usually enjoyable present which rushes on from minute to minute with fatal speed; the future, dim and uncertain, for which one can make any number of interesting plans, the wilder and more improbable the better, since–as nothing will turn out as you expect it to do–you might as well have the fun of planning anyway; and thirdly, the past, the memories and realities
